paragraphs.text: Parallel: Megaleh Amukos, VaEschanan, ofen 124 — “Yehoshua began to fight Amalek, whose power is the dog … therefore Esther said, ‘from the power of the dog, my only one’ (Megillah 15b), for she called Achashverosh a dog.” The Kabbalistic tradition also names Amalek's power ‘dog.’ It ties this to the Purim story: the kelipah that Esther faced in Achashverosh's palace is the same dog-kelipah that Adar's war on Amalek must break.

paragraphs.text: Gloss to Zohar II 121b, preserved in Mikdash Melekh — “'You shall throw it to the dog'—note: The female aspect of the Other Side is called kelev, dog, the reversal of bakol, 'in everything.'” The exact marginal wording is preserved here in the Zholkva 1864 edition. Rav Tzadok explicitly attributes it to R. Chaim Vital also in Pri Tzaddik, Mishpatim 9; that passage was retrieved as a witness to his attribution. The gloss's own digital text is marked 'note' without naming its author.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 109a — “Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Elazar said: They divided into three groups. One said: Let us ascend and dwell there; one said: Let us ascend and worship idols; and one said: Let us ascend and wage war. Those who said, 'Let us ascend and dwell there'—Hashem dispersed them. Those who said, 'Let us ascend and wage war' became apes, spirits, demons, and night spirits. Those who said, 'Let us ascend and worship idols'—'there Hashem confused the language of the whole earth.'” The Gemara lists the four forms resulting from the rebellious war against Heaven. Their correspondence to the middle line of holiness is developed at length in the author's cross-reference, Pri Tzaddik, Mishpatim 9.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra Rabbah 35:4 — “Statutes through which I engraved the heavens and the earth, as it is said: 'If not for My covenant by day and night, I would not have appointed the statutes of heaven and earth.' Statutes through which I engraved the sun and moon, as it is said: 'Who gives the sun for light by day, the statutes of the moon and stars for light by night.' Statutes through which I engraved the sea, as it is said: 'When He set the sea its statute.'” The Midrash reads the Torah's statutes together with the ordered laws of Creation. It develops the previous section's principle that the Divine order precedes Israel's observance.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Kedoshim 2 — “The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: Since you were sanctified to My Name before I created the world, be holy as I am holy. ... To what may this be compared? To a king who betrothed a woman. He said to her: Since you have been betrothed to my name, I am king and you are queen. As is my honor, so is your honor, because you are my wife. So the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moshe: Go and sanctify the people.” The Midrash presents holiness as the consequence of Israel's prior bond with God's Name. Rav Tzadok reads 'as I am holy' as the human task of becoming distinct from mundane attachment.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra Rabbah 24:8 — “Rabbi Avin offered another interpretation: It is like the people of a province who made three crowns for the king. What did the king do? He placed one on his head and two on his children's heads. So each day the beings above crown the Holy One, blessed be He, with three sanctifications. What does He do? He places one on His head and two on Israel's heads, as it is written: 'You shall be holy,' and 'Sanctify yourselves and be holy.'” The two sanctifications given to Israel make the crowns an image of its bestowed vocation. The same section explains their double portion through their struggle against the inclination, which the upper beings do not face.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra Rabbah 24:6 — “Rabbi Yehudah ben Pazi said: Why is the section of forbidden relations adjacent to the section 'You shall be holy'? To teach that wherever you find a boundary against forbidden relations, you find holiness. Rabbi Yehudah ben Pazi likewise said: Anyone who sets a boundary against forbidden relations is called holy.” This explicit connection between restraint and holiness supports the maamar's sequence from Shevat's repair of appetite and the covenant to Adar's kuf, 'holy.'

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Parshas Shekalim 12 — “Shevat was formed with tzadi, the time to repair the tzaddik's flaw … then comes Adar, formed with kuf, ‘kuf kadosh,’ set apart for wiping out Amalek, the opposite of the tzaddik's holiness.” The same order of months appears there, and it adds a step. The repair of Shevat and the kedushah of Adar together prepare for Nissan, ‘in which they are destined to be redeemed.’

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Seitzei 9 — “Rabbi Yudan bar Gadya said: Remember what he did to us concerning circumcision, which is situated in a person's lap. ... What did the house of Amalek do? They cut off the circumcisions of Israel and threw them upward, saying: Is this what You chose? Take what You chose. This is 'Their insult, with which they insulted You, Hashem.'” The Midrash makes Amalek's assault an insult against God's choice expressed through the covenant. Rav Tzadok treats the physical desecration as the form of its accusation against Israel's covenantal holiness.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II 23a, Vaera — “'I also established My covenant with them, to give them the land of Canaan'—because they were circumcised. Whoever is circumcised inherits the Land, for only a righteous person inherits the Land, and whoever is circumcised is called righteous, as it is written: 'Your people are all righteous; they shall inherit the land forever.' Whoever is circumcised and guards this covenantal sign is called righteous. Come and see from Yosef: throughout his days he was not called righteous until he guarded that covenant, the holy covenantal sign. Once he guarded it, he was called Yosef the righteous.” The passage includes both the covenantal sign and its guarding. Rav Tzadok quotes its initial statement in explaining the ground of Amalek's accusation and the holiness Israel must bring into expression.

paragraphs.text: Sefer Yetzirah, Gra recension 5:7, 10 — “He made the letter heh rule over speech, bound a crown to it, and combined them with one another. Through them He formed Aries in the world, Nisan in the year, and the right foot in the person, male and female.” The same recension assigns tzadi, eating, and Shevat together, and kuf, laughter, and Adar together. Rav Tzadok interprets this sequence of letters and months as a movement from disciplined appetite, through Israel's holiness, to the revelation symbolized by heh in Nisan.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Resisei Layla 58 — “The end of all the holiness of times that Yisrael establish—excluding Shabbos, which is fixed and permanent; after it there is no further holiness of time until Rosh Chodesh Nissan.” Resisei Layla gives the place of Adar in the year. As the last month, it completes the holiness that comes from Yisrael's side, and Nissan opens a new order.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Machshavos Charutz 19 — “Shabbos is called a ‘good gift,’ for it is holiness fixed and permanent from Hashem Himself … and a Yom Tov, which Yisrael sanctify, is also called Shabbos, for fixed holiness was drawn down to them.” Rav Tzadok explains there how the two holinesses meet. Yisrael's effort to bring holiness draws down the fixed holiness from above. This is why Rosh Chodesh Adar on Shabbos makes holiness easy to reach.

paragraphs.text: Bamidbar Rabbah 10:1; Pesikta Rabbasi 23 — “Rabbi Tanchum son of Rabbi Chiya said in Rabbi Yochanan's name: It is written, 'Sanctify My Shabbosos.' Through what do you sanctify it? Through food, drink, and clean clothing. What is written with it? 'They shall be a sign between Me and you, to know that I am Hashem your God.' I am Hashem, faithful to pay you your reward.” The retrieved Pesikta likewise reads 'to sanctify it' as food, drink, and clean clothing. These concrete actions are Israel's active participation in Shabbos holiness.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 6b — “Rabbi Tavi said: The reason of Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel is that bringing one redemption close to another is preferable. Rabbi Elazar said: His reason is from here: To confirm this second letter of Purim.” The discussion explains why Purim is observed in the second Adar of a leap year, adjacent to Nisan and the Exodus. Rav Tzadok reads that liturgical-calendar adjacency as the movement from Adar's work toward Nisan's redemption.
